intro: The cellos dance in five beats, two followed by three, with the ease of a waltz. A B-minor middle brings a repeated timpani note beneath the melody.

sections.label: A · Cellos dance in five
sections.mNote: A D-major cello tune over plucked strings

sections.label: B · B minor over repeated D
sections.mNote: Timpani and basses keep pulsing beneath the descending tune

sections.label: A′ · The D-major dance returns
sections.mNote: The cello tune recovers its light accompaniment

sections.label: Coda · Falling woodwind scales
sections.mNote: The close remembers the middle section’s descending phrases

cues.title: Cellos dance in five
cues.text: The cellos sing a D-major tune above plucked strings. Each bar holds five beats, grouped as two and three. Clarinets and bassoons answer with little falling phrases; the horns fill the gaps.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, pp. 11–13: opening cello melody, wind accompaniment and the five-beat dance. https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A four-hand version first
cues.text: In August 1893, while still scoring the symphony, Tchaikovsky makes a four-hand piano arrangement of it himself. Jurgenson publishes the piano duet in November 1893 and the full score in February 1894.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky Research, Symphony No. 6: the arrangement made between 1/13 and 12/24 August 1893, and the publication history. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6

cues.title: The last page of sketches
cues.text: At the end of this movement’s sketches, Tchaikovsky writes: “Today 24 March finished the rough sketches completely!!!” It is 1893, and he has already drafted the other three movements. The gentle dance is the last piece of the symphony to fall into place.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky’s inscription in the second-movement sketches, dated 24 March 1893 Old Style (5 April New Style); composition order documented at https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6.

cues.title: The timpani stay on D
cues.text: The middle turns to B minor. Flute, first violins and cellos carry a descending melody while timpani and double basses repeat D beneath it. Tchaikovsky’s marking asks for sweetness and a plaintive voice: con dolcezza e flebile.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 14, reproduces the middle-section score; the expression marking is discussed in Harlow Robinson’s note, https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: D major again
cues.text: The opening dance returns in D major. Its tune still fits five beats with extraordinary ease, and the plucked accompaniment puts spring back beneath the long notes.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, pp. 11–14, describes the return of the opening dance. Tonal plan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Woodwinds on the way down
cues.text: Descending woodwind scales lead into the coda. The middle section’s falling phrases return to the D-major dance, softened for the close.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 14: descending woodwind scales and the coda’s recollection of the middle section. https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Five beats over a single note
transitions.to: B · B minor over repeated D
transitions.how: The D-major dance turns towards B minor. Timpani and double basses settle on repeated D, while flutes, first violins and cellos descend above them. The five-beat bar stays intact; the new marking, con dolcezza e flebile, asks for sweetness and plaintiveness.
transitions.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 14; marking in Harlow Robinson’s programme note, https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6.

transitions.title: The dance regains D major
transitions.from: B · B minor over repeated D
transitions.how: The repeated bass note releases its hold, and the opening tune returns in D major with its plucked string accompaniment. The melody stretches across the same two-plus-three bar that carried the B-minor middle.
transitions.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, pp. 11–14; D-major reprise in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: Falling scales soften the close
transitions.how: Woodwinds descend in scales as the returning dance quietens. The coda recalls the middle section’s falling phrases within the D-major close; the five-beat accompaniment carries on beneath them.
transitions.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 14. https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf

source.title: Tchaikovsky, Symphony No. 6, II, historical full-score scan
source.locator: PDF p. 1 opening cello melody; p. 9 rehearsal D and repeated timpani; later return and pp. 23–25 coda. Times are passage estimates.

timeline.note: Opening dance: cellos sing above pizzicato support; clarinets, bassoons and horns colour the phrase.
The outer dance’s later build adds trumpet punctuation to winds, horns and strings (score PDF pp. 6–7); broadly placed before the measured 2:20–2:25 crest.
Middle region: flute and violin melody above repeated D, with timpani and lower-string support.
Return region: the opening dance’s melodic and accompanimental roles recover the foreground.
The returning dance rebuilds its wind, horn and trumpet reinforcement before the report’s 6:40–6:45 crest; a broad score-proportion state.
Coda region: quieter wind phrases and strings recall the middle section’s colour before the D-major close.
Coda brass phrase: trumpets and alto/tenor trombones enter above the D foundation (score PDF p. 24); broadly placed in the 7:25–7:45 renewed closing activity.
After the brief brass phrase, the reduced ending withdraws (score PDF p. 25); the report drops markedly at 7:50. Timing is passage-level.

composer.epithet: He could make a ballroom glitter, then let one unguarded melody tell us who was unhappy there.
facts: School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck: an allowance, 1877–90, and a friendship conducted by letter
Three ballets; Eugene Onegin, The Queen of Spades and other operas
composer.background:
At Kamenka on 6 July 1878, Tchaikovsky was explaining to Nadezhda von Meck how he composed. Ideas arrived in the middle of conversations; he held them in his head until he could sketch them on the first sheet of paper that came to hand. Waiting for the right mood was no way to work. “Inspiration is a guest who does not like to visit the idle,” he told her. Then he broke off for dinner. At two o’clock he resumed, moving on to sketching, orchestration, fair copies and how far a symphony must keep to its traditional form. Here is the composer of extravagant passions in his own voice: observant, companionable, exact about his trade.

He was born in Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. He grew deeply attached to his French governess, Fanny Dürbach, and began piano lessons at the end of 1845. The profession chosen for him was the law. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg. Four years later his mother died of cholera. He graduated in 1859 and took a post at the Ministry of Justice, while opera and concerts increasingly claimed his attention.
